passage:
Didi, you asked about my warning letter. You know how in Class 8 those guys used to hide my bag and call me "Hemu the Hippo", every day? And there's this new kid, Omkar: small, thick glasses, stammers when he reads. Last week one of them laughed at him and I... joined in. Then I started it myself. I called him "Owl". I pushed his books off the desk. Everyone laughed with me, not at me. It felt safe? Like I'd climbed out of the hole. Yesterday I saw Omkar eating lunch alone behind the water tank, the same place I used to hide. And I felt sick. Your little brother Hemant is doing to him exactly what they did to me. I don't know how to stop without looking weak.
Didi sat close and listened. "What they did to you was never your fault. Tonight we tell Mummy; tomorrow, your class teacher, about Omkar too."

qa.q: What did Hemant start calling Omkar?
qa.a: "Owl".

qa.q: Why did mocking Omkar feel 'safe' to Hemant?
qa.a: After years as the target, being on the laughing side felt like climbing out of the hole; the powerful role seemed to protect him from being picked on again.

qa.q: What could Hemant do next to stop without 'looking weak'?
qa.a: Stop the name-calling, apologise to Omkar privately, and, as Didi planned, tell Mummy tonight and the class teacher tomorrow about both what happened to him and what he did; stopping takes more strength than joining in.

qa.q: What is it like for Omkar to eat lunch alone behind the water tank?
qa.a: Probably lonely and frightening, the same hiding place and pain Hemant once knew.

grounding: A teenager who was bullied for years tells his sister he has started mocking a weaker boy because the powerful role feels safer, sees he is repeating the harm, and his sister responds that same day.

I'm Saurabh, and I've been in Chetan's section since Class 6. Back then the older boys made Chetan do their homework and flicked his ears on the bus. He never told anyone, as far as I know. This year he's in Class 10 and taller than most of us, and something's changed. Now he's the one on the bus making a Class 7 boy, Nikhil, sit on the floor. Yesterday he grabbed Nikhil's tiffin and passed it around. Some people laughed. I didn't know what to do.
I can't tell what's going on in Chetan's head. But I saw him look out of the window afterwards, jaw tight, the way he used to when it was him on the floor.
Today I told our class teacher what I'd seen on the bus. She said she would speak to both of them, and the bus in-charge, this afternoon.

qa.q: What did Chetan grab from Nikhil yesterday?
qa.a: Nikhil's tiffin, which Chetan passed around.

qa.q: What might Chetan's tight jaw at the window suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: Perhaps a flash of old hurt or guilt, seeing Nikhil where he used to be, even while he played the powerful role.

qa.q: Which choice of Saurabh's was the right one, and why?
qa.a: Telling the class teacher what happened on the bus, because Nikhil needed protecting and Chetan needed an adult to step in; the teacher acted that same afternoon.

qa.q: How might Nikhil experience the bus rides now?
qa.a: He likely dreads them, feeling humiliated and helpless on the floor, much as Chetan once did.

grounding: A classmate sees a boy who was once tormented now humiliating a younger student, and reports it to a teacher who acts the same day.

passage:
September. At his new school, Pankaj kept his head down. At his old one he had been shoved into lockers as "the fat boy" for two years. He still flinched when anyone raised a hand near him.
November. Pankaj had made friends, loud ones. In the canteen, one of them pointed at Dinesh, a small Class 8 boy who carried a violin case, and Pankaj called out, "Oi, Fiddler!" The table roared. Pankaj felt warm, part of something. The next day he said it again, louder.
December. Uma Ma'am, the class teacher, called Pankaj in after she found Dinesh crying by the stairs. "Dinesh told me what's been said," she said. Pankaj stared at the floor. "I know what that felt like," he whispered. "I'm doing it anyway." Uma Ma'am nodded. "Then let's work out how you stop, and how you put it right with Dinesh. Both your families will hear from me today."

qa.q: What had Pankaj been called at his old school?
qa.a: "The fat boy".

qa.q: Why did mocking Dinesh make Pankaj feel 'warm, part of something'?
qa.a: After two years as the target, being on the laughing side made him feel safe and accepted among loud friends.

qa.q: What choice did Uma Ma'am make, and why is it the right response?
qa.a: She acted the same day, listening to Pankaj without excusing him, planning how he stops and makes it right with Dinesh, and telling both families.

qa.q: What was it like for Dinesh to be called 'Fiddler' in the canteen?
qa.a: Humiliating and frightening, bad enough that he ended up crying by the stairs.

grounding: Over a term a boy who was bullied at his old school starts mocking a weaker student to feel safe, until a teacher steps in the same day it comes to light.

passage:
"Zubin, your principal called about the new student. Before your mother shouts, sit with your Ritu phuphi.
In Class 8 in Jaipur, three girls called me 'Rabbit' every day because of my front teeth. They held up two fingers whenever I answered. I cried in the washroom most afternoons.
Then in Class 9 a new girl came, Seema, with a patched bag from her elder sister. One day I heard myself say, loud, 'Nice bag. From a museum?' The same three girls laughed, with me for once. It felt like standing on dry land after a year in a river. So I did it again, and again.
One afternoon I walked into the washroom and Seema was there, crying, exactly the way I used to. I saw myself.
Being on the laughing side felt safe, beta. But it was the same cruelty, just pointed at someone new."

qa.q: What did young Ritu say about Seema's bag?
qa.a: "Nice bag. From a museum?"

qa.q: Why did mocking Seema feel like "standing on dry land" to young Ritu?
qa.a: After a year of being teased, joining the laughing side made her feel safe and accepted for once, far away from being the victim.

qa.q: What turning point made Ritu see what she was doing?
qa.a: Finding Seema crying in the washroom exactly as Ritu once had, which showed the same harm being repeated on someone new.

qa.q: What was Class 9 like for Seema?
qa.a: As a new girl with a hand-me-down bag, Seema was mocked again and again and ended up crying alone in the washroom, just as Ritu once did.

grounding: Shows, through an aunt's memory, a teenager who was tormented turning to mock a weaker newcomer, because the powerful side felt safer, until she sees the harm repeating.

passage:
The school bus broke down on the highway in May heat, and forty boys sat sweating for an hour while the driver waited for a mechanic. Bored, the back seat looked for entertainment.
Pradeep, fifteen, got there first. "Oye, Chaitanya! Still carrying your mummy's steel dabba? Want me to cut your chapati for you?" Chaitanya, small and new, pulled his tiffin closer. The back seat hooted. Two of those boys had spent all of Class 8 calling Pradeep "Chotu" and knocking his books into puddles. Now they were laughing with him, slapping his shoulder.
It felt good. It felt safe. So Pradeep kept going, louder.
Then he saw Chaitanya's fingers, white around the tiffin handle, trembling. Pradeep knew that grip. He had held his own bag exactly like that, on this same bus, two years ago. He stopped mid-sentence. The heat pressed down, and nobody said anything.

qa.q: What did the back-seat boys call Pradeep in Class 8?
qa.a: "Chotu".

qa.q: Why did mocking Chaitanya feel safe to Pradeep?
qa.a: The same boys who once tormented him were now laughing with him, so being the one who mocks felt far safer than being the target again.

qa.q: What turning point could let Pradeep break the pattern?
qa.a: Recognising Chaitanya's trembling grip as his own from two years ago; stopping there, and later saying sorry, would end the repeating harm.

qa.q: What is the hour on the bus like for Chaitanya?
qa.a: Small, new and stuck in the heat with nowhere to go, Chaitanya is mocked by a whole back seat and probably feels frightened and humiliated.

grounding: Illustrates a formerly bullied teenager who, on a stranded bus, mocks a smaller new student because the powerful role feels safer, repeating the harm he once suffered.

passage:
Diary. Hrithik.

Last year they called me "Tuh-tuh-Tiger" because of my stammer. Every single day. I used to eat lunch in the toilet.

Today a new boy joined, Sonam, from Sikkim. He has an accent. When he said "vegetable" wrong, I copied him really loudly. Everyone laughed. At me, WITH me. First time. I felt big. Safe.

Then Pallavi said, just to me, "That's exactly what they did to you." I didn't answer.

After lunch Mrs Pinto called me in. She'd heard. She didn't shout. She asked me how it felt last year. I told her about the toilet. Then she asked how Sonam might feel. She's calling both our parents today and wants Sonam and me to talk tomorrow with her there.

I don't feel big now. I feel sick. I did the same thing to him.

qa.q: What did Hrithik eat lunch in last year?
qa.a: In the toilet.

qa.q: Why did mocking Sonam make Hrithik feel big and safe at first?
qa.a: After being the target last year, being on the laughing side felt powerful and protective, like escaping the victim role.

qa.q: What was right about Mrs Pinto's response?
qa.a: She acted the same day, helped Hrithik connect last year's pain to Sonam's, called both families, and set up a supported talk.

qa.q: How might Sonam have felt being copied loudly on his first day?
qa.a: Sonam likely felt humiliated and alone, much as Hrithik had felt the year before.

grounding: Shows a teenager who was bullied beginning to mock a weaker student, taking the powerful role and repeating the harm, and an adult stepping in the same day.

passage: In the village school near Sitapur, last year the older girls had teased Uma every day because her father cleaned the drains. This year Uma was in class nine, and a small new girl, Devika, arrived in a torn uniform. At break, Uma pointed at the tear and called her "Rag Rani." The other girls laughed. It felt good. For once, Uma was on the side that laughed. Devika pulled her dupatta over the tear and stared at the ground. Their teacher, Mrs Ansari, had heard. She called Uma to the staffroom straight after break. "Last year, how did you feel when they talked about your father?" Uma's face went hot. "Bad." "Devika feels that now." Mrs Ansari sat with Devika at lunch, and that afternoon brought the two girls together to talk. She also sent a note home to both families before the school closed.

qa.q: What did Uma call Devika?
qa.a: "Rag Rani."

qa.q: Why did mocking Devika feel good to Uma at first?
qa.a: After being teased last year, being on the laughing side felt powerful and safer than being the victim.

qa.q: Why was Mrs Ansari's response effective?
qa.a: She acted at once, helped Uma remember her own pain, supported Devika at lunch, brought them together and told both families the same day.

qa.q: How might Devika have felt pulling her dupatta over the tear?
qa.a: Devika probably felt ashamed and small, trying to hide from the laughter.

grounding: Shows a teenager who was once tormented mocking a weaker student, repeating the harm, and a teacher stepping in the same day.

passage:
Last year in Valencia, Sofia had eaten lunch in the toilets to avoid the girls who called her "Sponge" for her curly hair. This year, at the new school, she had finally made it onto the popular table.

So when Mina, the new girl from Seoul, read aloud in class with a careful accent, Sofia heard herself say, loudly, "Ooh, robot mode." The table laughed. It felt like standing on the safe side of a wall.

By Thursday she was doing it every day. Mina started eating lunch alone, near the toilets.

Ms Ortega kept Sofia back after class that afternoon. "I've heard the robot comments. They stop now." Then, more gently: "Does it feel safer to be the one laughing?" Sofia's throat tightened. "Last year," she whispered. "Then you know how Mina feels," Ms Ortega said. "Tomorrow you'll apologise, and I'm checking on Mina today."

qa.q: Where did Sofia eat lunch last year?
qa.a: Sofia ate lunch in the toilets.

qa.q: Why did mocking Mina feel safe to Sofia?
qa.a: After being tormented last year, Sofia felt anxious about being a target again, and being the one laughing felt like the safe side of the wall.

qa.q: What did Ms Ortega do that could break the cycle?
qa.a: Ms Ortega stopped the comments firmly that same day, asked gently what made it feel safer, arranged an apology and checked on Mina.

qa.q: What is it like for Mina this week?
qa.a: Mina feels mocked and shut out, and starts eating alone near the toilets, the same place Sofia once hid.

grounding: Shows a teenage girl who was bullied last year beginning to mock a new student, until a teacher stops it the same day.

passage:
In Class 8, the seniors in the Ooty school hostel had made Harish sing to the wall at night and hid his shoes before PT. He never told anyone.

Now he was in Class 10, and Thomas, a skinny Class 7 boy, had joined his dormitory. On the second night Harish said, "New boy, fold my blanket," and the others laughed. Thomas folded it. The next night Harish added, "Now sing."

Standing there, arms crossed, Harish felt big for the first time in two years. He also felt something sour in his stomach.

The house warden, Mr Kurian, heard the singing from the corridor and walked in. "Enough. Thomas, go to bed." He took Harish outside. "Who did this to you?" Nobody had ever asked. "Class 8," Harish muttered. "Then you know how it feels," Mr Kurian said. "It stops tonight. Tomorrow we talk properly, with the counsellor."

qa.q: What did Harish order Thomas to do on the second night?
qa.a: Harish said, "New boy, fold my blanket."

qa.q: What was Harish feeling standing with arms crossed?
qa.a: Harish felt big and powerful for the first time in two years, but also something sour, a hint of guilt.

qa.q: Why was Mr Kurian's response wise?
qa.a: He stopped it at once, protected Thomas, asked Harish what had happened to him, and arranged the counsellor for the next day, so both boys get help.

qa.q: What is it like for Thomas in those first nights?
qa.a: Thomas is frightened and humiliated, obeying because he's new and small, the way Harish once was.

grounding: Shows a hostel boy who was bullied by seniors starting to bully a younger boy, and a warden who stops it that night.

passage:
Dear Pankaj dada,

Remember how I cried every day in Class 9 when Riddhi's group called me "Bidisha the Buffalo"? Well, I have to tell you something bad.

This year there's a quiet girl in Class 8, Moumita, who reads very softly. Last week I started imitating her whisper in the corridor. My new friends laughed. And for once I was on the laughing side. It felt so much safer. I did it again on Monday. And Tuesday.

Today Moumita cried in the library, and our class teacher called me to the staff room the same afternoon. Ma'am said it had to stop, and that she was phoning Ma. She was right. I had become Riddhi.

I'm apologising to Moumita tomorrow, with Ma'am there. Can you call me tonight? I feel awful.

Bidisha

qa.q: What did Riddhi's group call Bidisha in Class 9?
qa.a: Riddhi's group called Bidisha "Bidisha the Buffalo".

qa.q: Why did imitating Moumita feel safer to Bidisha?
qa.a: Bidisha had been hurt and humiliated in Class 9, and being on the laughing side felt like protection from ever being the target again.

qa.q: What steps now can help repair the harm?
qa.a: Apologising to Moumita with the teacher present, talking it through with Ma and Pankaj dada, and stopping the imitation completely.

qa.q: How might Moumita feel this week?
qa.a: Moumita likely feels humiliated and alone, crying in the library after being mocked in front of others.

grounding: A teenager who was once bullied writes about starting to mock a younger student, and the teacher's same-day response.

passage: Suraj, you said the boys who teased you now tease someone else, and you've joined in? Let me tell you about your Hemant chacha at fifteen. In the hostel, the seniors made me polish their shoes and called me "chuha". When I became a senior, I did the same to a thin boy from Bihar. It felt good, I'm ashamed to say. Like I had finally climbed out of the pit. One night the warden caught me, and instead of shouting, he asked, "Hemant, who made you polish shoes?" I couldn't answer. That same night he told my father, and the next morning he made me apologise to the boy. I never did it again. You don't climb out of the pit by pushing someone else into it, beta.

qa.a: "Chuha."

qa.q: Why did bullying the younger boy feel good to young Hemant?
qa.a: After being humiliated, taking the powerful role felt like climbing out of the pit; he felt safer, though he is ashamed of it now.

qa.q: How might the thin boy from Bihar have felt?
qa.a: Humiliated and trapped, just as Hemant once felt.

The school bus was stuck in a January fog jam, forty minutes late, and everyone was restless. Last year, on this same bus, Shalini had been "Chashmish", the girl whose glasses got snatched and passed around. This term she had moved to the back seat with the loud group.
When Gautam, a small Class 8 boy, climbed on with his oversized tiffin bag, Shalini called out, "Here comes the walking suitcase!" The back seat roared. She felt a rush, like finally being on the safe side of the laugh.
Gautam hunched over his bag, ears red, and stared at the fogged window. For a second Shalini saw herself there last year, clutching her glasses. She looked away and laughed louder.

qa.q: What did Shalini call Gautam?
qa.a: "The walking suitcase".

qa.q: What did Shalini feel when the back seat laughed?
qa.a: She felt a rush of relief and power, like finally being on the safe side of the laugh, with a flash of guilt when she remembered herself last year.

qa.q: What could help break this pattern?
qa.a: Shalini could act on that flash of recognition, stop and apologise to Gautam, and a teacher or bus attendant could step in and support both students.

qa.q: What is the bus ride like for Gautam?
qa.a: He feels humiliated and alone, hunching over his bag with red ears, just as Shalini once felt.
